checks.them: Okay, let's move on to some Android fundamentals. What happens when a child coroutine fails? When do you use SupervisorJob?

card.problem: Coroutine failure and when to use SupervisorJob
card.heard: child coroutine fails; when to use SupervisorJob
card.say: When a child coroutine fails, it cancels its parent, and the parent cancels all its other children. So one failure can stop the whole scope. SupervisorJob changes that: a failing child doesn't cancel its siblings or the parent. I use it for work that should stay independent, like separate day cards in a stream. One bad card shouldn't kill the rest.

card.problem: Coroutine failure and when to use SupervisorJob

One bad card shouldn't kill the rest.

results.detail: PASS: SAY correctly explains that a failing child cancels its parent and siblings under a regular Job, and that SupervisorJob keeps siblings independent, with a relevant example and no resume-topic contamination.

checks.them: StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel: which one for one-time UI events?

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events
card.heard: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events
card.say: For one-time UI events, I'd use a Channel or a SharedFlow. StateFlow is for state, so it always holds a value. A new collector would get the old event again, like an old error message. A Channel delivers each event once, to one collector. SharedFlow with replay zero also works, and it can have several collectors.

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events

results.detail: PASS: SAY compares all three for one-time events — StateFlow replays the latest value (old error message), Channel delivers each event once to one collector, and SharedFlow with replay zero works — and picks Channel/SharedFlow with a reason, in short spoken form.

checks.them: Why do we use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events
card.heard: Why use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?
card.say: repeatOnLifecycle starts collecting when the screen is visible and stops it when the screen goes to the background. Without it, a Flow keeps collecting while the user can't see the screen, so we waste work and can leak the view. With it, a StateFlow just gives the latest value again when the user comes back, so nothing is lost.

checks.them: What survives process death? How do you restore the screen?

card.problem: What survives process death and how to restore the screen
card.heard: What survives process death and how to restore the screen

When the user comes back, I read them and rebuild the screen.

checks.them: Let's switch gears to some live coding. Write a function that takes a Flow of String of SSE text chunks and emits complete events. A chunk can cut an event anywhere.

card.problem: Live coding: turn a Flow of SSE text chunks into a Flow of complete events
card.heard: Live coding: Flow of SSE chunks to complete events
card.say: Okay, I'll write a Flow operator that keeps a buffer of the text so far. On each chunk I append it, then split on the blank line that ends an event. Every complete piece before that separator is emitted, and the leftover stays in the buffer for the next chunk.
card.type: add@SseEventParser: fun Flow<String>.sseEvents(): Flow<String> = flow { ⏎     val buffer = StringBuilder() ⏎     collect { chunk -> ⏎         buffer.append(chunk) ⏎         while (true) { ⏎             val end = buffer.indexOf("\n\n") ⏎             if (end == -1) break ⏎             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) ⏎             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) ⏎             emit(event) ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }

card.constraints: ["Core scope: text chat, streaming, stop and history; photo and voice come later", "Draw the main layers of the app and say where the data lives", "Focus on the client and state what is needed from the backend"]
card.heard: User taps Stop — what happens on phone and server?
card.say: On the phone, I cancel the streaming job and keep the text already saved. The message stays in the database with a "stopped" flag, so the UI shows it as stopped. On the server, I call the stop endpoint with the message id, so it stops generating and saves what it has. The server would need to treat a late chunk after stop as a duplicate and drop it.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, thanks for joining. I'm one of the Android engineers here. Let's start easy: tell me about yourself in two minutes.
Candidate: Good morning, I'm Jianhui.
Candidate: I have ten years of experience in software development, mainly working on Android apps.
Candidate: Over the past three years, I've also been working on AI products, from development to launch.
Candidate: My most recent job was at KKday, a travel platform in Asia.
Candidate: I worked on the main features of the Android app and made the app run faster.
Candidate: Before KKday, I worked at Kezhi Technology, an AI education startup.
Candidate: I was the only Android engineer there.
Candidate: I built the Android app and worked with my team to launch the first version in just four weeks.
Candidate: That's also when I started working on AI features myself.
Interviewer: What did you build most recently on Android?
Candidate: Most recently, at KKday, I worked on the product page where users choose a package and options.
Candidate: Every tap recalculated all the prices and stock on the main thread, so it felt slow.
Candidate: I prepared the price and stock data in advance, moved the heavy work to a background thread, and sent results through StateFlow.
Candidate: Tap to finished screen went from about one second to 300 milliseconds.
Candidate: I also brought Jetpack Compose into the project.
Interviewer: Walk me through the SSE itinerary feature at KKday, from server to screen.
Candidate: Sure.
Candidate: The user enters a destination, a budget and a number of days.
Candidate: The backend agent picks places and bookable products, then streams the plan back day by day.
Candidate: On Android, the first day card shows up while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: Each card is checked before it reaches the screen, and a failed check retries, then falls back to a safe default.
Candidate: On the app side, I read the stream with OkHttp and parse each event as it arrives.
Candidate: Each day card goes into a StateFlow, so the list grows while the rest is still coming.
Candidate: If the connection drops, I reconnect and skip the days I already have.
